## Vocabulary

- **self**: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD (15/4)

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] A meta-analysis of therapeutic massage for motor symptoms in PD (Kang et al.; 363 participants in seven RCTs and one randomized pilot-control study) reported greater total effectiveness than control (RR: 1.33, 95% CI 1.14–1.55) and better UPDRS-III scores (SMD = −0.46, 95% CI −0.67, −0.24) but no better daily-living outcomes (SMD = −0.15, 95% CI −0.40, 0.10, p = 0.23), and a separate systematic review of 12 studies (Angelopoulou et al.) concluded that, despite methodological concerns, there is a wide range of safe massage techniques with beneficial effects on both motor and non-motor symptoms of PD. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9483027/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32147033/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Two systematic reviews found no significant advantage of acupuncture over placebo acupuncture on the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS): the Lee et al. review in Movement Disorders (eleven RCTs) pooled three placebo-controlled RCTs (n = 96, WMD, 5.7; 95% CI -2.8 to 14.2, P = 0.19) and judged the evidence 'not convincing', and the Noh et al. meta-analysis (42 studies involving 2625 participants) reported that its results failed to show acupuncture significantly more effective than placebo acupuncture in total UPDRS. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18618661/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28917379/
- [statement] In Yan et al., a single-center double-blind RCT in China that randomized people with PD and sleep complaints to real or sham acupuncture for 4 weeks (83 enrolled, 78 analyzed), Parkinson Disease Sleep Scale (PDSS) scores rose more with real than sham acupuncture after 4 weeks of treatment (19.75; 95% CI 11.02-28.49; P < .001), while the authors report that no statistically significant improvements in motor symptoms and daytime sleepiness were observed among the secondary outcomes. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11208974/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13189933/
- [statement] Trial reports and reviews state that acupuncturists cannot be blinded and that the evidence base is geographically concentrated: Yan et al. note the nature of acupuncture resulted in the acupuncturists being unblinded; Cui et al. state that acupuncturists could not be blinded, that the evidence base is small and predominantly from China, and that the predominance of positive findings raises the possibility that effects may be overestimated if negative or null trials remain unpublished; and Yu et al. state that full double-blinding was rarely feasible and allocation concealment was often inadequately reported. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11208974/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13189933/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12488745/
- [statement] Evidence-quality statements on massage in PD are cautious: Kang et al. report approximately 42.9% low risk, 42.9% some concerns and 14.3% high risk of overall bias and note that complete blinding of participants and personnel was impossible; Angelopoulou et al. cite methodological concerns, say longitudinal studies are needed, and report that Yin Tui Na technique combined with acupuncture was associated with worse motor scores; and Parkinson's UK says research suggests massage may help to reduce pain, anxiety and depression, although there is no conclusive evidence. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9483027/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32147033/, https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/information/treatments/complementary-therapies
- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017) recommendation 1.7.4 reads 'Consider the Alexander Technique for people with Parkinson's disease who are experiencing balance or motor function problems', and Parkinson's UK states that NICE clinical guidelines recommend that people with Parkinson's consider the Alexander technique to help with balance or motor problems (a page whose footer says 'Last updated November 2018'). (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD · also: https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/information/treatments/complementary-therapies
- [statement] Parkinson's UK states that there is little scientific evidence that complementary therapies can slow, stop or reverse the development of Parkinson's and that it does not endorse any particular therapies, while the Parkinson's Foundation says some therapies have even shown promise in Parkinson's studies but research is still in the initial stages and that acupuncture is also sometimes used to alleviate PD pain. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/information/treatments/complementary-therapies · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD · also: https://www.parkinson.org/blog/awareness/complementary-therapies

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Meta-analyses of acupuncture combined with conventional treatment report better UPDRS results than the comparison arm while describing the evidence as limited: one meta-analysis (42 studies involving 2625 participants) found that combined acupuncture and conventional medication showed significant improvements in total UPDRS, UPDRS I, UPDRS II and UPDRS III compared with conventional medication alone and rated the methodological quality of the RCTs low, and Yu et al. (50 RCTs, n = 3,248; acupuncture modalities combined with standard PD therapy) report acupuncture significantly outperforming Western medicine across all UPDRS domains while stating that the overall certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to low across most outcomes. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28917379/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12488745/
- [statement] In a three-group RCT in ninety-three people with idiopathic PD (24 lessons in the Alexander Technique, 24 sessions of massage, or no additional intervention), the Alexander Technique group improved compared with the no additional intervention group on the Self-assessment Parkinson's Disease Disability Scale at best (p = 0.04) and at worst (p = 0.01), with the comparative improvement maintained at six-month follow-up; a systematic review of Alexander Technique lessons (Woodman and Moore) concluded there was moderate evidence in Parkinson's-associated disability, and Parkinson's UK describes the evidence as one study of fewer than 100 people. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12428818/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22171910/, https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/information/treatments/complementary-therapies
- [statement] Sources differ on electroacupuncture added to anti-parkinsonian drug therapy: the Cho et al. guideline reports that in three RCTs electroacupuncture and anti-parkinsonian drugs, compared with drug therapy alone, showed no significant difference in overall clinical effectiveness and grades it 'may be considered' (strength C, level of evidence low), whereas Yu et al., in an analysis of 50 RCTs (n = 3,248), report that among all modalities electroacupuncture showed the highest overall efficacy. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6196228/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12488745/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Sham-controlled RCTs of acupuncture for PD-related fatigue found no significant difference between real and sham acupuncture: Kluger et al. (ninety-four PD patients, 6 weeks of biweekly treatment) reported significant improvements in both groups at 6 and 12 weeks without significant between-group differences, and Kong et al. (forty PD patients, 5 weeks) reported the same pattern; the Cui et al. review found fatigue showed no difference from sham (SMD 0.10) and graded certainty for fatigue very low. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27028133/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5853635/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13189933/
- [statement] Authors differ on what sham-controlled acupuncture results imply: Kluger et al. conclude that PD-related fatigue joins the conditions that acupuncture helps primarily through nonspecific or placebo effects, and Kong et al. judge real and sham acupuncture equally effective for PD-related fatigue and likely due to nonspecific or placebo effects, whereas Kwon et al. report that sham acupuncture combined with conventional medicine was superior to conventional medicine alone in their network meta-analysis and suggest that a sham acupuncture-controlled design might underestimate the effect of acupuncture treatment. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27028133/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5853635/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8619200/
- [statement] No serious adverse events were reported in the acupuncture trials and reviews read, although mild-event reporting was inconsistent: an earlier meta-analysis, Kluger et al. and Cui et al. each report no serious adverse events; Yan et al. report no severe adverse events in either group, with the most common self-reported acupuncture-related events being severe tremor; bleeding, numbness, or infection; and sharp pain during treatment; Cui et al. note that reporting of mild adverse events was variable and often not described in detail; and Parkinson's UK lists slight pain, bleeding or bruising, and feeling sick, drowsy or faint as minor, short-lived side effects. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28917379/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27028133/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13189933/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11208974/, https://www.parkinsons.org.uk/information/treatments/complementary-therapies
- [statement] Appraisals of the acupuncture-for-PD literature rate its quality low: an overview of 11 systematic reviews and meta-analyses (Huang et al.) rated all included reviews very-low-quality on AMSTAR-2, with GRADE revealing 20 studies with very-low-quality evidence, 9 with low-quality evidence, 3 with moderate-quality evidence, and 0 with high-quality evidence, and its authors say their conclusion must be interpreted cautiously; the York CRD abstract of the Lee et al. review reports that seven RCTs were of low quality, and Noh et al. rated the methodological quality of their included RCTs low. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7482669/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD · also: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK76307/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28917379/
- [statement] The complementary-medicine clinical practice guideline for idiopathic PD (Cho et al.) grades concomitant use of acupuncture and anti-parkinsonian drug therapy as 'should be considered' (strength of recommendation B, level of evidence low; twenty-one RCTs) and moxibustion as 'may be considered' (strength C, level of evidence low). (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6196228/ · keywords: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD

## Research summary — Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD

Evidence read for acupuncture, massage, the Alexander Technique and other traditional adjuncts in Parkinson's disease (PD). Two older meta-analyses found no significant UPDRS advantage of real over placebo acupuncture; later syntheses of acupuncture combined with conventional treatment report UPDRS gains but describe the evidence as limited, and an overview rated all included reviews very-low-quality. Sham-controlled trials show a sleep signal and no fatigue benefit over sham. No serious adverse events were reported. Massage meta-analyses report motor benefit alongside methodological concerns. NICE NG71 says to consider the Alexander Technique for balance or motor function problems; a complementary-medicine guideline grades acupuncture added to drugs 'should be considered' on low-level evidence; Parkinson's UK does not endorse any particular therapies.

## Source disagreement — Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD

Kluger et al. and Kong et al. attribute the improvement seen in both arms of sham-controlled fatigue trials to nonspecific or placebo effects, while Kwon et al. suggest a sham acupuncture-controlled design might underestimate the effect of acupuncture treatment.

## Source disagreement — Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD

For electroacupuncture, the Cho et al. guideline reports no significant difference in overall clinical effectiveness in three RCTs, whereas Yu et al. report that electroacupuncture showed the highest overall efficacy among all modalities.

## Source disagreement — Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD

For the Yan et al. acupuncture trial, Cui et al.'s study-characteristics table lists 161 participants, whereas Cui et al.'s narrative text states that the trial recruited 78 participants and the Yan et al. report states that 78 patients completed the intervention and were included in the analysis.

## Open question — Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD

Which participant count the Cui et al. review used for the Yan et al. trial in its pooled sleep analysis is not stated in the text read here.
